name: postal-code-field
title: Postal code field
description: A postcode field that knows the country: it writes 1234 AB, SW1A 1AA or 90210 the way that country does, and says what a valid code looks like when yours is not.
docs: country is the ISO code (NL, GB, US) and the field takes that country's pattern, placeholder, keyboard (digits for 90210, letters and capitals for 1234 AB) and spacing from a table of thirty countries. Nothing is forced while typing, so the caret never jumps: when the field is left, the code is written the way its country writes it (1017cj becomes 1017 CJ, 902101234 becomes 90210-1234), and from then on a wrong code is explained live, with what a valid one looks like (Dutch postcodes look like 1234 AB.), until it is right; a right one gets a quiet check. value, defaultValue and onValueChange(code, { valid }) work with the code as the country writes it once it is valid, and with the text as typed (trimmed) until then, so a draft kept in state, or posted through name, is never a string nobody typed. Changing country checks the code that is there against the new country at once (a code that is also right there is rewritten in its style) and reports the new answer. required adds aria-required and, once the field has been left empty, says what to enter (Enter a Dutch postcode, like 1234 AB.); like the other fields it never blocks a submit. A country without a rule accepts any text and shows no message. name adds a hidden input with the code the field reports, and the field carries autocomplete postal-code. countries adds or replaces rules ({ adjective, term, example, alternative, pattern, format, numeric }), and POSTAL_CODES, formatPostalCode, isPostalCode, describePostalCode and askForPostalCode are exported from postal-code-field/postcodes, so an address form or a server can share the table. A code is judged by its shape only: it can be well formed and still belong to no street.
